query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys to form a stable, protective oxide layer above 900 °C is controlled by the nature of the minor element X. When X is an element that forms low‐diffusivity, chemically inert oxides (e.g., Al or Si), the selective oxidation process produces a thin, coherent oxide layer with low lattice mismatch that grows slowly without cracking. In contrast, when X is an element (e.g., Mn) that oxidizes rapidly into a higher‐diffusivity, less adherent oxide, the resulting scale is thicker, less coherent, and prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state with a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Introduce the minor element X as either Al, Si, or Mn into the CrFeCoNi base alloy, with a direct comparison to CrFeCoNi alloys lacking the additional element.
generation.conditions: Exposure to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres for extended durations that mimic service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The interface between the metallic substrate and the oxide layer, specifically the lattice coherence and the matching of thermal expansion coefficients, moderated by grain boundary diffusion and interfacial stresses.
generation.mechanism: The oxidation mechanism is governed by the chemical affinity of X for oxygen coupled with its diffusivity in the alloy. For Al or Si, the lower diffusivity and favorable thermodynamics lead to formation of a slowly growing, adherent oxide phase (alumina or silica/silicate) with minimal interfacial strain. For Mn, rapid oxidation and high oxygen diffusivity result in non-protective, porous manganese oxides that cannot maintain coherence with the substrate, thereby leading to cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high temperature oxidative conditions, CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiSi alloys will form a thin, uniform, and slowly growing oxide layer that adheres well to the substrate, while CrFeCoNiMn alloys will develop a thicker, less coherent oxide that cracks and spalls, leading to accelerated degradation.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloys without the additional minor element X.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys operating at or above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres, and where the microstructure remains a single or multiphase metallic solid solution during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of interfacial strain and diffusion rates on the oxide scale’s growth kinetics remains to be fully determined, and additional microstructural factors may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of CrFeCoNiX samples with X = Al, Si, and Mn, along with a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy. Subject all samples to prolonged high-temperature oxidation tests (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere. Monitor the oxide scale evolution in real time using in situ high-temperature XRD and perform subsequent ex situ analyses (SEM, TEM, thermogravimetric analysis) to characterize scale thickness, adhesion, and integrity.
measurements: Rate of oxide layer growth (thickness vs time)
Morphology and coherence of the oxide/substrate interface
Occurrence and density of cracks or spallation
Phase identification of the oxide scales (e.g., alumina, silica, manganese oxides)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Mn-containing alloy produces an oxide scale that is comparably thin, coherent, and slow-growing as those formed on the Al- or Si-containing alloys, or if the Al- or Si-containing alloys develop non-protective, rapidly growing oxide scales with severe cracking/spallation.

Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction

Abstract: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract: Nb–silicide based alloy will require some kind of coating system. Alumina forming alloys that are chemically compatible with the Nb–silicide based alloy substrate could be components of such systems. The intermetallic alloys Nb1.7Si2.4Ti2.4Al3Hf0.5 and Nb1.3Si2.4Ti2.4Al3.5Hf0.4 were studied in the cast, heat treated and isothermally oxidised conditions at 800 and 1200 °C to find out if they are alumina scale formers. The alloys were designed using the alloy design methodology NICE and were required (i) not to have stable solid solution phase in their microstructures; (ii) not to pest and (iii) to form alumina scale. An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
